case_study_insert.main_stem: Kirsi Home Stores (KHS) is a private limited company in the home furnishings e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2014 by Kirsi Salo, the business sells flat-pack furniture and decor through its website, and operates a hierarchical structure with laissez-faire leadership. KHS plans to invest $700,000 in an automated furniture warehouse and a new dropshipping platform, financed by a $350,000 bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $192,000 a year, a variable cost of $16.00 a unit and a selling price of $48.00, and currently produces 16,000 units a year. KHS faces two problems: delivery damage complaints have reached 7% of orders and stock-outs are rising as demand grows.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: The warehouse dispatched 4,000 furniture orders last quarter, with a 7% damage-related complaint rate, down from 11% a year earlier. Stock-outs affected 5.4% of listed lines. Average delivery time is 5.6 days. A survey of 650 customers found 57% choose free delivery over speed, and 42% would pay $25 more for flat-pack sustainable furniture. The repeat-purchase rate is 29%, and the online conversion rate is 2.7%. HR is comparing a formal induction programme with mentoring by experienced warehouse staff to cut the 7% damage rate.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kirsi Home Stores as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank cut the base rate from 5.0% to 4.5%, lowering borrowing costs for KHS's $350,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage rises 5.8% to $13.40 an hour from April 2026, affecting KHS's workforce of 40. (3) Flat-pack timber and courier input costs rose 8.9% year-on-year, while consumer spending on home furnishings grew 1.6% and fuel surcharges add 3.2% to delivery costs.

questions.question_text: KHS is funding its $700,000 warehouse with a $350,000 bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for KHS of using the bank loan rather than only retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $350,000 bank loan preserves KHS's $350,000 retained profit as a cash reserve against fixed costs of $192,000 a year and a 7% damage-related complaint rate that forces refunds and replacements. Keeping that reserve is prudent while stock-outs are rising and inventories stand at $205,000, giving Kirsi Salo flexibility to buy stock or handle a delayed launch without exhausting internal cash.

Point 2: Borrowing lets the whole $700,000 automated warehouse and dropshipping platform proceed at once rather than waiting to accumulate profit, so KHS can capture the 42% of surveyed customers who would pay $25 more for flat-pack sustainable furniture. With the base rate cut from 5.0% to 4.5%, loan interest is cheaper than it was, making debt an attractive way to fund the project while the 1.6% growth in home-furnishing spending offers a chance to win new demand. A lower interest burden also supports the $28.00 average total cost and leaves more cash for the 5.6-day delivery operation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KHS's costs, reserves, complaints and expansion.

questions.question_text: KHS wants to cut the 7% delivery damage rate as it grows. Consider running its own delivery fleet, using a third-party courier, or switching to dropshipping. Which should KHS choose for delivery? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Own delivery fleet: Controlling delivery in-house lets KHS set careful handling standards, directly attacking the 7% damage-related complaint rate and protecting the $48.00 selling price from refunds. It also supports the 57% of 650 surveyed customers who choose free delivery over speed. However, buying vehicles and employing drivers adds fixed costs on top of $192,000 a year and the $700,000 warehouse plan, and a fleet may be underused, so it is expensive for a 40-employee retailer.

Third-party courier: A specialist courier offers national reach, established logistics and variable costs that rise only with orders, which suits the new dropshipping platform and avoids heavy capital spending. The drawback is less control over how fragile flat-pack furniture is handled, which could keep the 7% damage rate high, and courier input costs have risen 8.9%, so charges may increase just as volume grows.

Dropshipping: Suppliers dispatch directly to customers, removing warehouse handling and much of KHS's stock risk, which eases the stock-out problem and cuts the need for the $700,000 facility. In practice KHS loses control of packing and timing, and a 5.6-day average delivery plus 7% damage suggests fragile items need close oversight; margins are also thinner, squeezing the $32.00 contribution per unit.

Recommendation: KHS should use a third-party courier with strict handling agreements and its own quality checks. It gives national scale without the fixed cost of a fleet and more control than dropshipping, which is rejected because it removes control of packing when damage is already 7%. An in-house fleet is rejected as too capital-intensive alongside a $700,000 investment and 5.6-day delivery targets.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the delivery options with minimal application to KHS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KHS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of KHS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why a fleet and dropshipping are rejected.

questions.question_text: KHS's delivery damage complaints have reached 7% of orders and stock-outs are rising. Explain two benefits for KHS of clear downward communication in its hierarchical structure when tackling these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Clear downward communication lets Kirsi Salo and supervisors pass exact packing and handling instructions to the workforce of 40, so every worker follows the same method for fragile flat-pack items. Consistent instructions directly reduce the 7% damage-related complaint rate, protecting the $48.00 selling price from refunds and supporting the $700,000 automated warehouse investment, because new routines can be introduced quickly through the chain of command.

Point 2: Regular briefings downward keep warehouse staff informed about which lines are at risk of stock-outs and which have risen 5.4% of listings, allowing earlier replenishment requests to reach managers. In a hierarchical structure this formal flow of information makes responsibilities explicit, which suits laissez-faire leadership by giving staff clear standards while leaving them to solve problems, helping raise the 29% repeat-purchase rate as fewer customers receive damaged goods. Clear downward messages also reduce confusion over which lines are promoted online, protecting the 2.7% conversion rate.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to KHS's damage rate, stock-outs and structure.

questions.question_text: KHS wants to reduce the 7% damage rate among its warehouse staff. Consider a formal induction programme or mentoring by experienced staff. Which should KHS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Formal induction programme: A structured induction teaches all new warehouse staff the correct packing and handling routines from day one, giving a consistent standard that should reduce the 7% damage-related complaint rate. It is easy to document across the 4,000 orders handled each quarter and fits the hierarchical structure. The drawbacks are cost and time away from the line, and generic content may not address the specific fragile flat-pack problems that caused the 11% damage rate a year ago.

Mentoring by experienced staff: Pairing new workers with experienced packers gives practical, job-specific guidance on handling furniture, which directly targets the 7% damage rate without removing anyone from the floor. It supports knowledge sharing under laissez-faire leadership and costs little. However, quality depends on the mentor's own habits — bad practice can be passed on — and mentoring is hard to standardise for all 40 staff, so results may be uneven and slow.

Decision: KHS should choose a formal induction programme as the base, reinforced by short mentoring on the warehouse floor. Induction guarantees a consistent standard for every new starter, which is essential when 7% of orders are damaged and a $700,000 automated warehouse is being introduced. Mentoring alone is rejected as the main method because it cannot guarantee uniform practice; doing no structured training is rejected because the 5.4% stock-out rate and 7% damage show current routines are failing. KHS should compare the 7% damage rate before and after induction against the 11% figure of a year ago to judge whether the programme is succeeding.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of induction and mentoring with limited application to KHS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of KHS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering consistency, cost and job relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KHS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $192,000 ÷ ($48.00 − $16.00) = $192,000 ÷ $32.00 = 6,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 6,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $48.00 − $16.00 = $32.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $32.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KHS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 6,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 16,000 units to confirm the furniture range is profitable, leaving a margin of safety of 10,000 units, which supports the $700,000 warehouse investment.
2. Use average total cost of $192,000 ÷ 16,000 units + $16.00 = $28.00 a unit to track the cost of the 7% damage rate, setting a target to reduce refunds and lower unit cost toward $16.00.
3. Use contribution per unit of $32.00 to test the $25 premium sought by 42% of surveyed shoppers for flat-pack sustainable furniture, since each premium unit adds directly to profit on 16,000 sales.
4. Use labour productivity of 16,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 400 units per worker to benchmark the automated warehouse, linking the 5.4% stock-out rate and 2.7% conversion rate to output per employee before expanding further.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 6,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $32.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 16,000-unit output; average total cost of $28.00 to track the 7% damage rate; contribution analysis of the $25 premium; and labour productivity of 400 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KHS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KHS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.80 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.64 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $180,000 inventories + $50,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $270,000; 2025 current assets = $205,000 + $45,000 + $60,000 = $310,000. The 2024 figure is $270,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.80; the 2025 figure is $310,000 ÷ $165,000 = 1.88. Excluding stock, 2024 liquid assets are $50,000 + $40,000 = $90,000, giving $90,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.60; 2025 liquid assets are $45,000 + $60,000 = $105,000, giving $105,000 ÷ $165,000 = 0.64.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved on both measures. The 1.80 to 1.88 rise shows current assets cover short-term debts more comfortably, helped by cash rising from $40,000 to $60,000. The 0.60 to 0.64 improvement shows KHS is a little less dependent on selling inventory to meet debts, useful while it repays a $350,000 loan and funds a $700,000 warehouse. However, both stock-excluding measures remain well below 1, so liquid assets still fall short of liabilities, and inventories rose from $180,000 to $205,000 partly to guard against the 5.4% stock-out rate; with a 7% damage rate, some of that stock may be hard to sell, so the quality of the asset base is questionable.

Conclusion: KHS's financial position has improved, but only modestly. Both measures rose and the rise is not purely a stock build-up, since receivables actually fell from $50,000 to $45,000. The main weakness is low liquid cover, so KHS should keep tight cash control while investing the $350,000 retained profit and $350,000 loan in the new warehouse.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and cash movements and a justified conclusion on whether KHS's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KHS of selling flat-pack sustainable furniture as promoted in its market research.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Flat-pack sustainable furniture matches the 42% of 650 surveyed customers who would pay $25 more, letting KHS lift its $48.00 selling price and add to the $32.00 contribution per unit while appealing to the 57% who value free delivery and low prices. It also supports the $700,000 automated warehouse, because flat packs are compact to store and dispatch, helping reduce the 5.4% stock-out rate and the 7% damage rate.

Disadvantage: Sustainable materials and eco-packaging often cost more than standard inputs, raising the $16.00 variable cost per unit and eroding contribution unless the $25 premium is fully accepted; the insert gives no figure for this extra cost, so the benefit cannot be quantified. Flat packs can also arrive damaged or incomplete, and with a 7% damage-related complaint rate and 2.7% conversion, any quality slip would raise refunds and weaken the 29% repeat-purchase rate, so the 4.5% base rate is welcome as cheaper credit to fund the transition.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KHS's survey, costs and damage rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate cut from 5.0% to 4.5%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 8.9% rise in timber and courier input costs will affect KHS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate cut (5.0% to 4.5%): This is a favourable change. If KHS's $350,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost falls by 0.5% of $350,000 = $1,750 a year (0.005 × $350,000), easing the burden of fixed costs of $192,000 a year and freeing cash for the $700,000 warehouse. If the loan is fixed, the saving is delayed until refinancing. Lower rates may also support the 1.6% growth in home-furnishing spending, though the benefit is a modest, one-off gain rather than a change to unit costs.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.40 per hour): With a workforce of 40, this rise pushes up wage costs in warehousing and packing and is unavoidable. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented. The correct benchmark is the given productivity figure: 16,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 400 units per worker. If productivity holds at 400 units, the rise is absorbable; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $32.00 contribution per unit is squeezed at a time when the 7% damage rate already adds cost.

Timber and courier input inflation (8.9%): The insert does not decompose the $16.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole variable cost rose 8.9%, that adds 8.9% × $16.00 = about $1.42 per unit, or roughly $22,784 a year at 16,000 units. Courier inflation also makes the 7% damage problem more expensive to fix through returns, and with home-furnishing spending up only 1.6% and fuel surcharges adding 3.2% to delivery, KHS has limited power to pass costs on through its $48.00 price.

Conclusion: The 8.9% rise in timber and courier costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit, is far larger than the $1,750 interest saving, and directly threatens the $32.00 contribution that funds the $700,000 expansion. The wage rise can be offset if 400-unit productivity holds, and the rate cut is a benefit rather than a threat, so input inflation is clearly the dominant external change.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KHS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KHS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of KHS with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
